sets.title: Living with tourism
sets.transcript: Anyone who has tried to cross the historic centre of Rome on a summer afternoon will understand why the word overtourism has entered the dictionary. And yet the debate is rarely as simple as it's made out to be. Tourism pays for restorations, keeps thousands of small businesses afloat, and, let's be honest, has given many of us a living. The real problem isn't the number of visitors so much as their concentration: the same ten streets, the same three months. Some cities have experimented with entry fees or caps on short-term rentals, with mixed results. Perhaps the more promising approach is subtler: spreading visitors across lesser-known neighbourhoods and seasons, so that the city remains a place where people actually live, rather than a stage set they're merely passing through.

questions.prompt: What is the speaker's overall attitude to the overtourism debate?
options: It is more complicated than people suggest.
questions.explain: “The debate is rarely as simple as it's made out to be.”

questions.prompt: Which benefit of tourism does the speaker NOT mention?
questions.explain: Restorations and small businesses are mentioned; public transport is not.

questions.prompt: “…has given many of us a living” suggests the speaker…
questions.explain: To give someone a living = to provide their income.

questions.prompt: According to the speaker, what is the real problem?
options: Visitors are concentrated in the same places and months.
There are too many visitors in total.
questions.explain: “The real problem isn't the number of visitors so much as their concentration.”

questions.prompt: How does the speaker describe entry fees and rental caps?
What does “a stage set” suggest in the last sentence?
options: A place that only looks real, where no one actually lives
A theatre in the city centre
questions.explain: The speaker fears the city becomes scenery for visitors, not a home for residents.
